subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members of the house will have heard with regret of the death of the Prime Minister of India, a sister member of the commonwealth of nations. The death of Mr. Nehru is a loss not only to India and her people, who knew him best, but a loss to all mankind. Among the leaders of this century no one had made a greater impact on his time. No one has been more dedicated to the proposition that peace should prevail among nations and freedom should exist among men than the Prime Minister of India.
His talents and his energies were long devoted to the cause of India's independence, and when that was achieved he became a strong supporter of India's association in the commonwealth of nations. As the leader of his country his aim was to bring social justice and dignity to India's common man. He inspired respect amongst his adversaries, affection in his friends and confidence in his followers and admiration of all men.
Our sympathy, Mr. Speaker, goes out to his countrymen in their loss, to his colleagues in the government of India, and especially to his family.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Jawaharlal Nehru belonged to that select group of men who, in any day and generation, leave their imprint upon mankind. He was a man who was educated in the British tradition. He attended Harrow, graduated from Cambridge and became a member of the bar of the inner temple. Orator, political philosopher and scholar, Nehru was a man immortal while still living. The Prime Minister will find when he attends the meeting of the prime ministers of commonwealth countries a few weeks hence that sitting around the table there will be five or six representatives of various commonwealth countries who at one time or another served
terms in jails or penitentiaries for their activities on behalf of what they believed to be right.
Nehru fought for independence, as the Prime Minister has said, and having done so he then became a strong, powerful and devoted servant of the commonwealth as a whole. He gave to India or continued in India the British tradition of parliamentary government, the rule of law and above all the principles of freedom based on British justice. A man of commanding personality, a mystic, a political philosopher and a practical politician, he combined in himself the unusual number of ingredients necessary for political and national greatness. He had a sense of humour and at all times, as the Prime Minister has said, was devoted to the welfare of the average man.
India has lost its greatest. When I say that I am not unmindful of the tremendous contribution of Mahatma Gandhi. The commonwealth has lost a devoted friend and counsellor without whose dedication, following the achievement of India's independence, India would not have continued in the commonwealth of nations.
The world has lost a great figure, and I associate myself with the Prime Minister in extending our sympathy to the president and people of India, to the members of the immediate family and to his sister Madame Pandit, who for so many years strengthened his hand and stood with him amidst all the trials and tribulations that were his.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all lovers of democracy will be saddened at the death of Prime Minister Pandit Nehru. I think history will record him as one of the half dozen great statesmen of our century.
Pandit Nehru and Mahatma Gandhi were the architects of India's independence, and it is a tribute to their powers of leadership, as well as to British statesmanship, that India was able to move from colonial status to nationhood with a minimum of rancour and bitterness. It was typical of the man that he was able to say, after India had attained her independence, "I spent 11 years in a British jail but I have the highest regard for British

Tributes to Nehru
traditions," and he carried that regard into building a parliamentary democracy in the country whose freedom he had helped to bring about.
Today, in Asia, India is like a light upon a hill, a demonstration that it is possible without any diminution of democratic principles, to bring about economic advancement and social justice. It is significant that the last public speech Prime Minister Nehru made was a plea for better relations between India and Pakistan, a plea directed not to Pakistan but to his own people to show the tolerance and forebearance which alone could establish a new basis for discussion.
Mr. Speaker, democracy has lost a great champion. India has lost a great leader. I am sure all hon. members of the house will extend to the government and the people of India their deepest sympathy in this sad hour in their nation's history.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, India and the world have lost a truly great man. The late Prime Minister Nehru was not only one of the outstanding statesmen in this post-world war II era but also the champion of democratic parliamentary government, leading India from colonialism to independence to become the largest democratic country in the world.
Certainly it was no small achievement to have built this former colony into a democratic nation, giving the right of the free vote to more than 400 million people. His selfless dedication and courageous determination were directed to all mankind and to the peaceful development of his country and the world.
We in this party join with the Prime Minister, with all hon. members of the house and I am sure with all Canadians in extending our sympathy and regrets to the government of India, to the people of that great country, and to the Nehru family.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the beloved leader of a friendly country is no more.
Mr. Nehru was the beloved leader of a friendly government. He was also the supporter and champion of all worthy causes, the defender of the weak, the friend of oppressed countries and a relentless worker on behalf of peace in the world.
Without being a narrow minded nationalist, Mr. Nehru espoused the cause of any

oppressed country, the same way he undertook to fight for freedom in his own country.
As he said himself:
We do not seek to dominate any country and we do not want to meddle in other people's affairs. Our main task in world affairs is to maintain peace and ensure that the equality of all races is recognized and that all people under foreign domination become free.
He believed in democracy, not the simple democracy that results from the free exercise of the right to vote.
Democracy, he said, means tolerance, not only of those who share our views but also and especially of those who do not.
His concept of freedom was not limited to political rights alone but it covered everything that contributes to the welfare of man.
True freedom, he said, is not purely political, it must also be economic and spiritual.
Mr. Nehru was the friend of the masses. He said one day:
Our main problem today is to raise the living standard of the masses, enable them to satisfy their needs, enable them to live decently and help them not only to enjoy material things but also cultural and spiritual values.
Not only the Indians, not only the people from Asia but all the men of the world, all freedom and justice loving men lose a defender and a friend.
So we join with the Prime Minister of our country (Mr. Pearson) in extending to the Indian people our deepest sympathy.

MR. PIGEON-RESOLUTION ON "VOTES AND PROCEEDINGS" RESPECTING FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
My remarks are based on the Votes and Proceedings of the house dated May 26, 1964, and on the answers given to the house by the Prime Minister in the past two weeks concerning a Canadian flag, and particularly on the reply which he gave to the question I put to him yesterday and which appears on page 3581 of Hansard.
Mr. Speaker, the answers given in the house by the Prime Minister in the past two weeks clearly suggested that the government would submit a resolution for the adoption of a Canadian flag and a Canadian anthem.
However, the resolution appearing in the Votes and Proceedings of May 26, 1964 asks, for various reasons, recognition by Canada of two flags and two anthems.
Mr. Speaker, in view of that resolution and the answers given in this house by the Prime Minister, I maintain that, by his wiliness and weakness, the Prime Minister has derided the Canadian people and, both by what he said and left unsaid, has misled the hon. members of this house.
That is why I want to express all the humiliation I feel as a result of such trickery and I am not afraid to say, at this stage of our proceedings, that such behaviour on the part of the Prime Minister could very well destroy mutual trust and respect, and spread confusion and dissension across Canada.

MR. ORLIKOW  PROCEDURES RESPECTING SECURITY INVESTIGATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. On Monday last the Prime Minister replied to my question dealing with the government's security investigations policy, to the effect that the government's policy had been approved and "formally communicated to all government departments and organizations", but that "It is not customary to send directives such as this to employees or associations, nor are administrative directives normally tabled in the House of Commons".
On October 25 last year the Prime Minister, in dealing with the many questions on this matter, announced that new procedures would be adopted. Apparently this has now been done. Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely

Question of Privilege
necessary that the government's policy should be given the widest publicity. The rights of Canadian citizens and government employees are more important than the privacy of a few government ministers or top civil servants. In the light of what has happened and what became apparent last week in Toronto, as exemplified in the Hooper case, we ail have a right to question whether top government civil servants are always concerned about the rights of ordinary people.
If the statement which the Prime Minister made during the last session had any meaning, we and the people of Canada have a right to know the policy with regard to security which has been evolved by the government, and this will not be done by keeping it secret except for a few high government officials. This policy should be given to this house publicly.

It seems to me that we should have, as a matter of privilege in this parliament, a clear indication of what are the security regulations which the Prime Minister promised the house would be brought into effect as a result of the discussions in this house during the last session.

subtopic: MEDICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR PRIVATE PILOT'S LICENCE
MEDICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR PRIVATE PILOT'S LICENCE
speechtext: Is consideration being given to amendment of medical requirements permitting the granting of a private pilot's licence to persons with monocular vision?

subtopic: MEDICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR PRIVATE PILOT'S LICENCE
speechtext:
No. Amendment of Canadian medical requirements along these lines on an unilateral basis would be inconsistent with our international undertaking to adhere to the minimum medical standards set up by the international civil aviation organization and which, in this respect, provide for a specific minimum of visual acuity in each eye separately and which consequently excludes a pilot with monocular vision.
The question of what privileges, if any, the pilot with monocular vision should have is highly controversial and, together with a number of other areas of difficulty in the application of the international personnel licensing requirements, we plan to seek an early review of these requirements by the international civil aviation organization.

subtopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN T.C.A. AND TRANSAIR
CONTRACT BETWEEN T.C.A. AND TRANSAIR
speechtext: Is the government satisfied that both parties have lived up to the agreement, signed by TransAir and Trans-Canada Air Lines, whereby TransAir was obliged to maintain passenger service for three years in return for certain aircraft and equipment being turned over to them?

subtopic: CONTRACT BETWEEN T.C.A. AND TRANSAIR
speechtext:
The agreement between TransAir Limited and Trans-Canada Air Lines was a private one and was only subject to air transport board scrutiny to the extent that its provisions were of assistance in determining whether the continued operation of the services in question was economically feasible.
Following public hearings, the board found in its decision dated March 18, 1964 that certain of the prairie services referred to in the agreement had occasioned TransAir Limited such substantial losses as to endanger the

Questions
continuation of the other prairie services operated by that carrier. The board, therefore, amended accordingly the route pattern set out in the licence of TransAir Limited.
Trans-Canada Air Lines has taken every required step to implement its part of the agreement. TransAir Limited is not in breach of the agreement, since it undertook "to operate on such route pattern as may be approved from time to time by the air transport board". In other words, TransAir has adjusted the route pattern of services referred to in the agreement with the approval of the air transport board as provided in the agreement.
Under the circumstances, the answer to the question is, yes.

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, May 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Martin (Essex East) for the second reading of Bill No. S-17, respecting the territorial sea and fishing zones of Canada.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Last evening I started on the first leg of my cruise of Canada's territorial seas and today I hope to finish the voyage.
From the facts I placed on the record it is readily apparent that Canada's support of a 12 mile limit was officially launched in the international field in 1958. However, international agreement on this matter was not reached and we are now obliged to consider the alternatives open to us. The first question which comes to mind concerns those nations which have already applied a 12 mile limit. We know, for example, that Iceland was the first country to push out its territorial limits to 12 miles, followed by Norway, Denmark and then Russia. Africa and Britain have also decided on this course and, in all, some 25 nations have now adopted a 12 mile limit. There should be little objection from these countries to the Canadian proposal. But it would appear that when these decisions were made unilaterally, international incidents followed. Icelandic gunboats chased British trawlers from cod fishing grounds off the shores of Iceland. Norway is chasing Swedish fishermen from grounds which the Swedes have fished for hundreds of years. Irish corvettes have recently scattered Dutch and Belgian fishermen who were fishing in Irish herring grounds, and the Brazilian and French are disputing the ownership of Brittany lobsters caught in traditional Brazilian fishing waters.
This will give the government an idea of what happens when action is taken unilaterally, and I cannot help but wonder what steps are to be taken by the minister and his department to enforce these proposed regulations. What would happen, for example, if the Russians decided to test the new regulation by placing a factory ship within the nine mile limit off the coast of Cape Breton

in an area where in the spring of the year the fishing is prolific? I refer to the Scatari bank. It might be that the factory ship would not be fishing in these waters, but the supply draggers would be travelling back and forth and it would require constant patrolling on the part of Canadian vessels to determine whether they were fishing or simply travelling peacefully through these waters.
I would point out, too, that Canada has a very long coast line. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin)-and I may point out that he is not present while this bill, which comes under his authority, is being discussed-

To continue, I ask this question: How does the government hope to enforce this regulation? Obviously, enforcement will be one of the main problems to be dealt with if these proposals are to become effective. I cannot impress this point upon the government too strongly. I have said before, and I say again, that a gunboat policy for our fishing industry would be disastrous to our traditional fishing markets. The entire proposal raises the problem of historic fishing rights and today I will deal only with those rights on the Atlantic coast. France and the United States have historic fishing rights dated back to the treaty of Utrecht in 1713 and the treaty of London in 1818.
I hold in my hand the brief submitted by the Fisheries Council of Canada on Canada's national and territorial waters under date January 28, 1963. In this brief they recommend negotiations between the United States and France to reach a mutual understanding, and that unilateral action be taken only after agreement with these two countries. The Fisheries Council of Canada is representative of the entire fishing industry. It meets annually and it makes recommendations to the government only after careful study of all the facts. I cannot help but wonder why these recommendations were ignored and why the government, despite their recommendations, decided to take unilateral action.
I think their suggestions are worth placing on the record. They suggest, for example, that Canada, as one of the pioneering nations in the field of international agreements for the conservation of fishery resources of the sea, should continue to provide international leadership and protection for our Canadian marine resources. They recommend that we declare certain bodies of water as Canadian national waters, and establish the straight base line to enclose the national waters. The breadth of the territorial seas and exclusive fishing zone would be measured seaward from the base line. We should recognize and negotiate historic treaty fishing rights and then make a unilateral declaration with regard to the decisions reached. Finally, we should enforce these progressive steps, thereby preventing all other foreign fishing, except the United States and France, from exploiting our marine resources. In my opinion it will be difficult to get some of these nations to give up and suddenly drop their historic fishing rights. The house therefore has a right to

Do they intend a phasing out of historic fishing rights over a five or ten year period; or, for example, will the Americans and the French continue fishing their traditional grounds within three miles of our shores in perpetuity? These are questions that require an answer.
Quite frankly, I am not satisfied that the present proposal as outlined by the minister will solve any of our major international fishing problems. In my opinion we will still have large Russian, Spanish and Japanese trawlers operating on the fishing banks of the Atlantic coast five, ten and 15 years from now in ever increasing numbers, using modern methods and equipped with electronic fish finding devices that can only be described as fantastic. I say this because the world population, according to statistics that were last prepared in the year 1960, I believe, was estimated at 2,900 million and it is increasing by 120,000 every day. The nations of the world must turn to the sea as a source of food in ever increasing quantities to feed their ever expanding populations, and as a result fishing operations will intensify in the years ahead. As a matter of fact, the world fisheries have doubled their production in the last ten years, and a further doubling in the next ten years is expected. This, of course, will only create further international competition on the high seas for our marine resources.
This is why I have stated that in my opinion further negotiation at the international level would have been preferable to the action that has been taken at this time by the government. However, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) of this government have decided in their collective wisdom to establish by unilateral action this 12 mile limit. Since the 12 mile limit is a conservation measure designed to assist our inshore fishermen as well as conserve our fisheries resources, it is therefore important that we take some definite steps at this time that will be of long term benefit to our fisheries.
In my opinion this measure is not definite enough at present to do what should be done for the Canadian fishing industry. However, it can be amended by the simple act of naming the co-ordinates or points of land to be used in establishing the base line. These co-ordinates are the key, the one important item in this entire proposal; but

I am hopeful, however, that our discussions will soon be completed and that the governor in council will be in a position before the end of the year to proclaim a list of geographical co-ordinates of points for application of the straight base lines to at least a part of our coast line. If our optimism, here, proves unwarranted it will not be because this is not our present appreciation of the situation; it will be because of the nature of the negotiations themselves. It is unlikely that the governor in council will publish points covering our entire coast line in his first list. It is possible that, depending on how our discussions proceed, he will publish several lists and that, in the first, base lines will come into force only for those areas in respect of which we have completed our talks.
Mr. Speaker, no one likes travelling through uncharted seas. If we accept this bill as it is now written, we allow this government to take the entire fishing industry on a cruise in the sea of uncertainty. The whole bill, in so far as my reading of it leads me to believe, is surrounded by a fog of indecision. It reminds me somewhat of the Liberal government. They do not know where they started from; they do not know where they are, and they do not know where they are going.

speechtext:
For example, base lines can be drawn from the United States border along the coast of New Brunswick, past the harbour of Saint John, and then back again along the coast of Nova Scotia, thereby leaving the entire bay of Fundy outside the territorial seas of Canada. Conversely, a base line can be drawn from the United States border to cape Fourchu, completely sealing off the bay of Fundy and St. Mary's bay, thereby conserving the sardine and scallop industry in the bay of Fundy and the new scallop beds and the inshore fisheries of St. Mary's bay, as these waters would then become part of Canada's internal, or national waters.
I could give the house other examples, but I believe the most important co-ordinates with which we are concerned at this time are those to be used in the Newfoundland-Cape Breton area. I believe, and the Conservative party supports the principle, that the base line should be drawn from cape North to St. Paul island and then to cape Ray in Newfoundland. A base line should also be drawn from cape Freels, Newfoundland, to cape Bauld and then to Labrador. This action would seal off the valuable fisheries

resources around Bonavista-Twillingate-and this should be of considerable interest to another maritime member, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill)-

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext: Winnipeg.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
-Notre Dame bay, and especially the fishing banks in the gulf of St. Lawrence. Bradell bank near the Magdalen islands, Orphan and Natashquin cod banks off Quebec, Centre bank off Labrador and the banks around Anticosti island, would all be protected. Mr. Speaker, I am not advocating that we draw an iron curtain between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, but I sincerely believe that, if the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence are classed as Canada's national inland waters, it will be the greatest forward step taken toward conservation of our fisheries resources in the history of this nation. This action would provide a giant spawning ground for all types of fish, and it would come entirely under the control of the Canadian government.
Since most of the sealing operations are also conducted in this area, it would also give the Canadian government complete control over this industry, which has been very much in the limelight during the past few months as a result of the methods used to catch the seals. There should be little objection raised by other nations to these changes, because they would indirectly benefit from our conservation measures. At present any conservation measures carried out on the high seas are completely under the control of the international commission for the north Atlantic fisheries. When we consider the pressure placed upon the ships operating on our offshore banks to bring back suitable catches, it is questionable whether they are following the recommendations of the commission. We must remember that some of these countries fish for food while we fish for profit.
Some evidence has been submitted that would indicate that fishing nets have been used with a mesh so small a sardine could not escape. We cannot, as Canadians, enforce regulations governing the methods to be used for catching fish on the high seas. However, if we seal off the gulf of St. Lawrence as a giant spawning area, and classify this large body of water as Canada's national waters, the offshore banks will eventually benefit from our conservation measures.
As I stated earlier, the co-ordinates to be used when implementing this measure are of vital importance, not only to the future

of our fishing industry but also to about nine international air lines which are concerned at the immense powers granted to this government or to future governments by this bill. As clause 5 of Bill No. S-17 now reads, the government could by order in council establish geographical co-ordinates which are far out in the ocean. This, of course, would cause international repercussions and would be difficult to enforce, but in the meantime great damage would be done. As this bill is now worded, notwithstanding the fact that its prime purpose is to assist the Canadian fishing industry, it could have a very serious effect on the operation of foreign international air lines flying across the north Atlantic ocean outside of the present territorial jurisdiction of Canada.
Canadian law on the subject of the operation and control of aircraft is set forth in the federal Aeronautics Act. The extent of this Canadian law is defined in the key operative sections of the act, which are sections 3 and 4. In each of these sections, in so far as foreign aircraft are concerned, the extent of the Canadian control is limited to flights over Canada and the territorial waters of Canada. This is consistent with international law and international conventions that have been entered into and to which Canada has been a signatory. Also under international law the territorial waters of a state-for the purposes of aeronautical law have been restricted to the customary three miles from the shore line. While the width of the territorial sea will still remain three nautical miles under this bill, I would point out that the inward point of measurement has been altered. The new definition of a territorial sea adopts the straight base line system for the purpose of measuring the width of the territorial sea at any given point on the coast line of Canada.
But where are these base lines to be drawn? This is what the bill states in clause 5 (1), (2) and (3), and I should like to place it on record:
(1)	The governor in council may, by order in council, issue one or more lists of geographical co-ordinates of points from which base lines may be determined and may, as he deems necessary, amend such lists.
(2)	In respect of any area for which geographical co-ordinates of points have been listed in a list issued pursuant to subsection (1) and subject to any exceptions in the list for the use of the low water line along the coast as the base line between given points, base lines are straight lines joining the consecutive geographical co-ordinates of points so listed.

It is in the method of determining the geographical co-ordination of points as outlined in clause 5 that the problem will arise in so far as its applicability to the Aeronautics Act is concerned.

The present government might quite properly deny that they had any intention of using Sable island as a geographical coordinate. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great attention to the remarks made by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse). He has referred to the recommendations made by the Fisheries Council of Canada, an organization which represents the Canadian fishing industry from coast to coast. As was stated by my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) when he introduced the bill, the discussions which have taken place so far with the ten countries interested in fishing in Canadian waters or in proximity to the Canadian shore, were based on the representations which were made to the government on January 28, 1963 by the council.
On April 20 of this year, while the Fisheries Council of Canada was having its annual meeting in Charlottetown, I had the opportunity of meeting the executive of this council. I want to state to the house that I received unanimous approval from the Fisheries Council of Canada of the action being taken by the government with regard to the 12 mile limit.
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg has made reference to Russian, Spanish and Portuguese vessels which will be fishing in proximity to the Canadian shore even though the 12 mile limit is introduced. It is true that they will have the right to fish outside of the 12 mile limit, and there are a number of fishing banks located outside of the 12 mile limit which are being frequented not only by Canadian fishermen but by fishermen from a number of foreign countries.
But the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, who is familiar with the fishing industry and has a personal interest, also knows that the 13 countries represented on the international commission of the north Atlantic fisheries, including all the countries operating on these banks which have been referred to by the hon. member, are subject to certain regulations and conventions for the conservation and preservation of our fisheries. This year the annual meeting of the international commission of the north Atlantic fisheries will take place in Hamburg during the month of June.
The hon. member has referred to the seal operation. As I have stated in the house before, and we have given notice already to this effect, we want the seal fishery of the north Atlantic outside of the 12 mile limit to

come under the protocol to ICNAF in order that we can have regulations which will be observed for the preservation and conservation of the seal herds which mean so much to a large number of fishermen of the Atlantic coast.
When this bill was before the other place a representative of the Fisheries Council of Canada answered a number of questions asked him by members of the other place and he stated that they were satisfied with the action taken by the government. In one breath the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg says that we are going too far. He is afraid of retaliation by our friends and neighbours, the Americans. In the next breath he says we should define immediately all the coordinates. The fact is that we have been negotiating on a 12 mile limit for the last seven or eight months. We have had a number of meetings with different countries, and it was generally agreed by the Canadian representative and the representatives of the other countries involved that it would not be proper to take a unilateral position now by defining specifically what the co-ordinates should be.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) announced in the house on June 4 last that it was the intention of the government to take action, he made it very clear that such unilateral action would be taken after discussions with the countries involved. I should like to quote part of the last paragraph of his remarks, as found on page 621 of Hansard, in which he said:
He also called attention to the "historic" and treaty fishing rights of the U.S.A., and I assured him-
He is referring to his meeting with the late President Kennedy at Hyannis Port:
-that these rights would be taken into account. Discussions will be held with the United States with a view to determining the nature and extent of the U.S.A. rights and interests which may be affected by the action which Canada is taking. Discussions will also be opened as soon as possible with other countries affected, and it is our hope and belief that we will be able to reach agreement with such countries on mutually satisfactory arrangements.
This is the position that Canada has taken after having been unsuccessful in obtaining a multilateral agreement on the law of the sea. I am not complaining because the previous government could not succeed in obtaining such agreement. They were not alone in this regard. There were a number of other counfries in the same boat. But when we saw it was impossible to come to such an agreement,
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones in order to prevent powerful foreign countries such as the U.S.S.R., Japan and others establishing historic rights which are recognized internationally and then having to deal with those countries as we are dealing today with other countries that really do have such historic rights, we decided that the time had come for Canada to take action, and we have notified the countries involved accordingly.
Negotiations are now under way. We have completed the first phase of negotiations and we are convinced that we will arrive at a satisfactory agreement. In order to do this it was important that the government should not only make known its intention to proceed with the establishment of a 12 mile fishing zone but that it should be given proper, enabling legislation which would provide the government of the country with the power to proceed with the establishment of such a zone.

speechtext:
National interest and international good will are to be considered in establishing new extended limits along our Canadian coast lines. While Canada is spending what it does for conservation, for the propagation of species, the extension of the limits to 12 miles and the establishment of a fishing zone seem to me to be sound business. It is, in fact, the kind of action which can be expected by other countries in similar positions. Under these circumstances the more amicable road of negotiation seems desirable and preferable. What we are doing now is to introduce by unilateral action what it has been impossible to achieve, as I said earlier, by international or multilateral convention.
I should now like to refer to the treaty rights which certain countries have in certain of our waters, and to the historic rights which are claimed by others. As has already been stated on several occasions by my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), and myself, United States fishermen will be permitted to engage in their traditional fishing operations on both coasts.
On the Atlantic coast the United States has treaty rights in addition to claims of historic fishing, and for this reason alone is entitled to special consideration in any arrangements on fishing within areas that will become either internal waters or the contiguous fishing zone.
On the Pacific coast, where Canada and the United States are the only two countries whose fishermen operate in the areas off the Canadian coast line, we have a long history of

co-operation with the United States in the development of fisheries of principal concern to the two countries, such as salmon and halibut.
These fisheries have been brought up to a sustained yield level and are being maintained, and in one case, that of salmon, increased by co-operative measures of the two countries and by the restrictions accepted by the fishermen of Canada and the United States for a number of years. Because of this historic intermingling of fishing operations, as well as the intermingling of the stocks of fish concerned, and the long established history of joint conservation measures, it is only fair that the interests of United States fishermen be recognized, and this applies on both coasts.
I want to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that this recognition would be contingent on United States recognition of reciprocal treatment to be accorded to our fishermen by the United States, should it decide to assume jurisdiction over areas off the United States coasts beyond the three mile limit, where our fishermen would be exploiting any stocks of fish. It is not our intention to tell our neighbours that we want them outside the 12 mile limit when we know-and I repeat what I have already said-that a number of our own fishermen on both coasts are also interested in fishing in United States waters. Had Canada been successful in its attempts during the past ten years to establish a 12 mile fishing zone by way of a multilateral convention, the normal procedure would have been for the government to seek from parliament implementing legislation following the signing of the convention. As this was not possible, the alternative of proceeding by way of unilateral action, coupled with negotiations with countries having fishing interests and this requires legislative authority. A mere declaration by Canada would not suffice. It would amount only to a declaration of intent and such a declaration on behalf of the government has already been made by the Prime Minister. I refer hon. members to the statement made on June 4, 1963. Legislation has now been introduced to give effect to that declaration, to show the countries interested that not only is it the intention of Canada to proceed with legislation establishing a 12 mile limit but that Canada has taken a decision on the matter and passed enabling legislation to establish a territorial sea and fishing zone. Enactment by parliament of this enabling legislation will be an indication of the national will expressed through parlia-
27, 1964
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones ment. At the same time, the bill provides the necessary flexibility to enable the government to take account of the final arrangements with the countries with which we are negotiating.
Reference has been made to the difficulty of enforcing such regulations. I might say to the hon. member that the adoption of the 12 mile fishing zone and the straight base line system will not add materially to the difficulties of enforcement. In some cases enforcement will be rendered easier. With the publication of charts delineating base lines it will be easier both for foreign fishing vessels and for our patrol vessels to get their bearings. Some difficulties of enforcement may be encountered but I may say we are prepared to meet such difficulties. Under the existing law it is almost impossible for Canada to enforce such regulations. We have had experience in recent months of cases where foreign vessels have been apprehended by Canadian patrols. The matter has come before the courts and we have found that we have difficulties in referring to specific legislation which determines whether such vessels were operating inside or outside the three mile limit.
At the present time we have a fleet of some 26 vessels which could be used to patrol both coasts. We have three large vessels on the Atlantic coast-the Cape Freels, the Cygnus, and the Arctica in addition to 11 vessels of medium capacity. On the Pacific coast we have four larger vessels-the Laurier, the Howie, the Kitimat and the Hunter besides eight vessels of medium capacity. We also employ air patrols on both coasts, and have exclusive use of two Beavers at all times during the fishing season on the west coast. On the east coast the use of helicopter S-55 plus a fixed wing aircraft is available as and when required. Again, I wish to assure the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse) that the matter he has raised in connection with air lines will not be a problem when the 12 mile limit is brought into effect.
I hope hon. members will realize the position in which the fishing industry of this country finds itself. I hope they will agree that it is time for Canada to go ahead and to take this unilateral position for the protection of our fishing industry.

As
the sponsor of Bill No. C-27, a bill to establish a 12 mile fishing limit which was put forward by the New Democratic party in this house- and, incidentally, I might say it was talked out at that time-I should like to say a few words on the legislation proposed by the government. Like several other members who have already spoken, I rise to take part in this debate as a member from the west coast, one who is concerned, just as the minister is concerned, with the welfare of the fishing industry and of its workers.
Both in the Atlantic and in the Pacific the establishment of a 12 mile fishing zone has long been sought as a means of conserving and harvesting our fishing resources. The measure before us in my view will not accomplish these objects. It is even true to say there are many in British Columbia connected with the industry who believe it may have an opposite effect. My study of the bill and my understanding of the explanations offered

to us so far prompt me to make the following brief criticism of the clauses of this measure.
In clause 2 it is declared that any other act of parliament or any order or regulation made shall have a preferred legislative position and shall not be interfered with by the provisions of Bill No. S-17 unless Bill No. S-17 so states. This means that under the provisions of this legislation at present the United States, for example, will continue to have fishing rights in Canadian waters and nothing is being done in the legislation before us to phase out those rights or change them. Further, nations which claim historic fishing rights may also have that privilege protected, because section 4 of the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act states that the governor in council may issue permits for foreign vessels to fish in Canadian waters whether as a result of a treaty or for any other reason. This means, it seems to me, that our American friends, for example, on the Pacific coast will have continued freedom to troll or drag for fish right up to the three mile limit. In effect, their ability to do so will be decided in practice by whatever pressure is exercised upon our cabinet. This bill further determines that the territorial sea and the fishing zones will be drawn on the headland to headland principle. However, clause 5 leaves these arrangements entirely in the hands of the government to proclaim by order in council. In other words, the government could, by order in council, change a fishing area or move it in or move it out just about the way the tide comes in or goes out.
This to me is a very wishy-washy piece of legislation and there are many people connected with the fishing industry in British Columbia particularly who are not satisfied with it in its present terms. On that point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read into the record briefly an editorial which appeared earlier this month in the Columbian, the New Westminster newspaper, which is headed, "Fisheries bill gutless". The article says:
Canada's much vaunted 12 mile fisheries bill is becoming more denatured and gutless every day.
The article goes on to say:
As debated so far, both the U.S. and France claim historic rights to continue fishing to the three mile limit. Only a few European countries would be restricted. In the Pacific, it is not known if Japan and Russia will honour the 12 mile limit, if the U.S. doesn't.
Canada would be spineless if it did not enact the protective regulations it wants off its own shores.
This means Canada would exclude everybody, including the U.S. and France, from fishing within

the 12 mile limit, subject to a modest transition period. Exceptions would be separate, mutual localized agreements, as for sharing the Fraser river fisheries.

subtopic: DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS ON CUMULATED REGIONAL PRICE BASIS
DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS ON CUMULATED REGIONAL PRICE BASIS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to amending the Agricultural Stabilization Act to:
(1)	provide deficiency payments for eggs, hogs, etc., on a cumulated regional price basis rather than on a national weighted average price;
(2)	have these deficiency payments made semiannually instead of annually as at the present time.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to introduce this resolution for

debate. This is not the first time I have placed this resolution on the order paper. I placed it on the order paper in the last two or three sessions, but it never reached the debating stage, although it is of great importance to the egg producers and hog producers of Canada.
As you will see from the motion, it provides deficiency payments for eggs and hogs on a cumulated regional price basis rather than on a national weighted price. Second, it suggests that these deficiency payments be made semi-annually or quarterly, instead of annually as at the present time. This is very important to the egg producers, because when the weighted average price in Canada is calculated the producers on the prairies never receive a deficiency payment.
For the record I should like to point out that in 1962 the average price in Canada was 34 cents per dozen. At that time there was a deficiency payment allowance of one cent per dozen. One cent per dozen for grade A large was received across the country. In Saskatchewan the average price over the year was 28J cents per dozen, and if the price had been calculated on a regional basis the producers would have received 5J cents to bring them up to the 34 cents. Instead of that they received only one cent because the average national price was 33 cents.
It is very important that these averages be calculated on a regional basis because there are times when the price of eggs goes down quite a bit. I put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) on this matter and received an answer today. As we all know, producers of eggs in Saskatchewan at the present time get as low as 17 J cents per dozen for their eggs. If the national average were 34 cents and deficiency payments were based on 34 cents, the farmer would be entitled to at least 13 to 15 cents per dozen. When the national average is taken across Canada and the price over the year in British Columbia and the west, or in Ontario, Montreal and the east, is 33 cents average, deficiency payments will amount to only one cent per dozen.
My argument is that we should pay the price calculated on a regional basis. Whether the regions are defined as the prairies, central Canada and then eastern Canada, or whether province by province, it is all the same. These deficiency payments should also be made, as I said, on a quarterly basis. Although my motion calls for a semi-annual basis, I should like to see them made quarterly. During the

last two campaigns the Liberals, realizing that this was a problem, promised a quarterly payment made on a regional basis if they were put in power. So as not to deceive anyone about this, these statements were made on May 3. Therefore all parties seem to be in favour of making deficiency payments on a regional basis instead of on a national weighted average price.
As far as hogs are concerned the matter is much more important. Everyone knows that in the fall when the farmers bring their hogs to the market prices are usually down. The farmers who are able to market their hogs in the spring always get a little better price. If deficiency payments are made on an annual basis it would mean that whatever deficiency payments were paid to the farmers who received low prices for their hogs in the fall they would be cancelled out by the payments received by the other farmers in the spring. This is an important issue. Promises were made by all parties during both election campaigns; this proposal has been advocated by farm organizations across the country; and I think that this is the time to pay attention to the question and to change the act. Actually, the stabilization board makes these payments from October 1 to September 30. That is the year for the calculation of these deficiency payments, and that is the year within which prices are averaged.
I am sure many other hon. members are interested in this very important proposal, Mr. Speaker, so I will not take up any more time in speaking to the matter. I conclude by urging on the Minister of Agriculture, under whose jurisdiction falls the stabilization board, to give consideration to this question; and in view of the fact that promises have been made by his party along the line I have suggested and the matter has been brought to his attention by members of other parties, I ask him to give serious consideration to making these payments on a quarterly basis.

subtopic: DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS ON CUMULATED REGIONAL PRICE BASIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with much attention to the opening remarks of the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) on the motion we are called upon to discuss today. 1 must admit that I found this motion very interesting and, at first sight, I thought it would greatly help the farm people in my riding. However, after studying it closely, and especially after making some inquiries, I had to change my mind for the following reasons. The motion reads as follows:
Agricultural Stabilization Act
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to amending the Agricultural Stabilization Act to:
(1)	provide deficiency payments for eggs, hogs, etc., on a cumulated regional price basis rather than on a national weighted average price;
(2)	have these deficiency payments made semiannually instead of annually as at the present time.
At present, the act provides that support prices will be established with respect to the nine following named commodities: hogs, cattle, sheep, eggs, butter, cheese, wheat, oats and barley not produced in the designated areas set up by the Canadian wheat board.
Under the act, the support prices are to be no less than 80 per cent of the average price for the ten previous years. The exact level, in terms of a percentage of the average for the ten previous years, may be set by the governor in council anywhere above 80 per cent but, as far as the named commodities are concerned, it must never be under 80 per cent.

May I point out here, Mr. Speaker, that support is not limited to the nine named commodities. The act permits the governor in council to provide price support on any other agricultural products. At the present time there is a total of 18 commodities being supported under the act. In the case of products other than the nine named ones, the support can be set at any level which the governor in council determines.
The act also authorizes the governor in council to designate the grades of any product to which support will apply. In the administration of the act there are three methods of providing price support. One is known as the purchase method. Under this method the stabilization board is authorized to buy any products of the approved grades offered to it at the support price. Since the board, under this method of support, is an open buyer of all products offered to it, that is indeed, in my opinion, an effective way of maintaining the price of the product at not below the support level.
This method of support, however, has certain very serious difficulties attached to it which are referred to later. It has therefore been discarded gradually for most commodities and the stabilization board now supports the price of only two commodities by the purchase method, these being butter and cheese.
A second method of support, which has been used in a few instances, is by compensatory payments. There are direct payments

Agricultural Stabilization Act on a unit of product. An illustration of this is the payment of 3.6 cents per pound which is made on first grade Cheddar cheese under the dairy support program for the current year announced a few weeks ago.
The third method of price support, and now by far the most common one, is the deficiency payment method. Under this method, if the average price to producers over the support year falls below the support price a direct payment is made to producers for the difference between the two. In applying the deficiency payment method the support price is established on the basis of an average price for the whole area in which the commodity is produced. Thus, for products produced all over Canada the support price is a national one based on the average national price over the 10 year period. Similarly, the price which producers receive, and which is used for determining whether a deficiency payment is necessary, is calculated on the basis of a weighted average national price received by producers. If at the end of the support year that weighted average national price is less than the national support price a deficiency payment is made.

This motion would change this method of computation of deficiency payments and would also change the length of time provided for those payments. It would change the method of computation in the sense that it would replace the present national price basis by a regional price basis. In addition, payments would be made semi-annually ininstead of annually as at the present time.
I have already mentioned that the stabilization board has now discarded the system of price support through the purchase method, except for butter and cheese. The reason for that is, that serious difficulties were experienced with most commodities where the formula was applied. That method led to surpluses very hard to dispose of, put the government in the position of buyer and seller of farm products and upset the normal process of production and marketing.
That method is still applied in the case of butter and cheese, because up to now we have not found any satisfactory alternative. You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the motion refers specifically to pork and eggs. Those two commodities actually provided striking examples of the complete impracticability of the price support system through the purchase method I have just mentioned. About four 
years ago, the board stopped buying eggs and pork and since then, support has been provided through deficiency payments.
One of the main difficulties involved in the purchase method to support prices was, as I said earlier, the problem of marketing huge production surpluses. As long as the government remained an open buyer of all commodities offered, there was no restriction, no check on production. Finally, when the government suspended the application of the abovementioned method, it discovered that it had in stock over a hundred million pounds of tinned pork, and it has just found the necessary outlets for the final disposal of that considerable stock.
A second difficulty of the so-called purchase method, and this applies to the motion now under consideration, was that it removed all incentive to the sale of farm products to any other outlet than the government even at a fraction of a cent below the support price of the government. If the government offered to buy pork in Manitoba, for example, at a fixed price of 22 cents per pound for pork, grade A, it is evident that nobody would sell pork at 21.5 cents per pound, even if there was a demand. Therefore, that represented a very serious restriction to what I would call the normal flow of trade, and that restriction was removed by the program of deficiency payments.

For the benefit of the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) and other interested members may I say that any consideration of applying deficiency payments on a regional basis would have to be certain to have to avoid at the same time that same difficulty of interfering with the normal flow of trade, as I mentioned in French a moment ago. In most agricultural products there is a normal pattern and flow of trade. There are areas which produce more than they can consume, and others which are deficient naturally. Even these surplus and deficiency areas are by no means static. They change, and an area which is in a surplus position at one time may be short at another time. Any action by government which interferes with this normal flow of trade could lead to difficulties.
I should like to point out that a regional price support, even under deficiency payment, could remove the incentive from the people in that area to get the best possible price for their product in any market open to them.

They would know that regardless of how low the price was the government would make up the difference.
I will agree with many hon. members that the present method of price support may not be perfect. In fact, no country has yet found a perfect method of supporting the price of farm products. The present method of providing deficiency payments on an annual basis and on a national average price certainly may not protect fully against temporary difficulties in some regions. But it does prevent distortions in the normal flow of trade, permits production patterns to adjust themselves to changing circumstances and, finally, ensures that producers on the average will be compensated if the average national price over the year falls below the national support level.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have come to the conclusion that it would certainly be premature to comply with the hon. member's wishes and change over to a regional basis, unless and until a method can be found to guarantee that such a basis would not create more difficulties than it could remove.
In closing, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for having introduced this motion which, even if it is not accepted by the house, will at least have allowed us to clarify certain points and become better informed about the numerous difficulties facing the farmers. That will enable the government to continue its progressive work in the field of agriculture to the greatest advantage of the Canadian nation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to offer a measure of support to the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) with regard to his notice of motion which we are discussing this afternoon. I think his contention that support prices should be established on a regional basis rather than on the basis of a national weighted average is a good one. However, I will have to disagree with the contention that has been put forward by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Berger) that there is a possibility of severe interference with the normal exchange of these commodities between regions. I think it is fair to say that, for the most part, what commodities are produced in a region, that is eggs, hogs and so on, are consumed in that region. I am not trying to confine this statement to a province or anything like that.
I remember back in the days when they had a floor price on hogs and they used the
Agricultural Stabilization Act purchasing method to support the price of hogs. The Calgary market is the one with which I am most familiar. At that time the support price for hogs in the Calgary market was based on the Toronto price less the freight. Almost all of the hogs that were coming into Calgary, and I think this applies to Edmonton as well, were either consumed in Calgary or they went to the west coast. The price of hogs in Toronto had nothing to do with the situation at all. There was very little, if any, of that pork that went from the western region to Toronto, but this was the basis of the support price that was paid in that market.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, the same argument applies to a large extent to eggs and a number of other things. I am not going so far as to say that every egg or every pound of pork produced in a region is also consumed there. I feel, however, that the amount of these products exchanged between regions is so small in relation to the total volume it would not present a problem at all. I want to say that I believe it would be far more fair to have these prices established on the basis of regional prices than national ones.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) for the initiative he has taken in presenting this motion.
I have done some research on the regional versus the national basis of providing deficiency payments on egg and hog prices, and with the help and co-operation of the stabilization board. I have come to the following conclusions. Since the deficiency payment method of supporting egg and hog prices was introduced, representations have been made to the stabilization board to the effect that the deficiency payments should be made on a regional rather than on a national basis. It has been claimed that producers in certain parts of the country would have received considerably larger amounts if the payments had been made on a regional basis.
In view of these representations the board has undertaken to calculate and compare the results of using both bases in the case of the egg support program. In this study separate calculations have been made for each of the nine provinces, and for Canada as a whole. This makes it possible to see what the results would have been if the payments had been made on a provincial as well as on a national basis.
In investigating this matter the first thing to remember is that, regardless of which

basis of administration we wish to consider, it is necessary to calculate two particular prices. In every case it is necessary to determine the prescribed or support price and the weighted average market price. Thus, in order to provide deficiency payments on a provincial basis, we must calculate the support price and the weighted average market price for each province. Any deficiency payment that would be paid to the producers of a certain province would be the difference between the support price and the weighted average market price of that particular province.
The following two tables show the base price, the support price, the weighted average market price, and the deficiency payment for each of nine provinces, and for Canada considered as a national unit, for the egg marketing years 1961-62 and 1962-63. Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask permission of the house to have these figures accepted as read, as I do not want to take all the time of the house on this matter. These are figures supplied to me by the stabilization board, comparing the prices and the results of their tests.

An examination of table I shows several things. In the first place it indicates that if the deficiency payments had been made on a provincial basis, farmers in the three prairie provinces and Prince Edward Island would have received a fraction of a cent per dozen more than they actually did; that farmers in Quebec would have received two cents per dozen more, and that those in the remaining four provinces would have received from a fraction of a cent to a cent a dozen less.
It is also evident that payment on this basis would have meant that producers in Quebec would have received a payment of three cents a dozen, whereas those in New Brunswick would not have received any payment at all. It may also be noted that, if payment had been made on a provincial basis, the amount would have been different in every province. This is in contrast to the complete uniformity of payment which exists when payments are made on a national basis.
Again it can be seen that if payments had been made on a provincial basis no producer in any part of the prairie provinces could possibly have received more than $24 extra income. This could only have happened in Alberta where a producer could have obtained .6 cents a dozen on a maximum of
4,000	dozens.
Finally, it is clear from an examination of the table that the mere act of shifting from

a national to a regional basis cannot possibly remove more than part of any inequality or unfairness that may exist in the distribution of deficiency payments. Moreover, this must be the case, regardless of the size or number of regions that might be chosen. While a division into nine regions corresponding with nine provinces might result in a slightly more equitable distribution, it certainly could not ensure anything like complete equity. The truth is that in order to get complete justice or equity in this matter, the calculations would have to be made on an individual farm basis, rather than on either a national or regional basis.
It is obvious, of course, that any program which involved the calculation of a separate payment for every individal farm would be hopelessly unwieldy, extremely expensive, and virtually impossible from the administrative standpoint. This last statement points to a very important reason for not using any regional basis of payment, namely the fact that it would greatly increase the complexity, the cost and the general difficulty of administration. Moreover, these difficulties would multiply as the number of administrative regions increased.
On the basis of ordinary logic, as well as the data shown in table I, I submit that a truly remarkable degree of justice can be obtained without resorting to anything more

complex, and from an administrative point of view, more difficult and expensive, than the national basis of payment.
However, regardless of which basis is or should be used, it seems desirable to try to explain precisely why the payments tend to be distributed differently when a regional basis of payment is used than when the national basis is used. For example, why would the use of the regional basis have increased the payment going to producers in each prairie province by a fraction of a cent a dozen, as indicated in table I? In order to explain this it is necessary to remember that the national weighted average market price is a price which reflects the quantity sold as well as the price received in each and every section of the country. It is especially important to realize that the variation in the quantity marketed in the different sections of the country played a very important part in determining the actual level of this national average price. In order to realize the real significance of this factor, it should be noted that there are approximately twice as many grade A large eggs marketed in eastern as in western Canada.
So, not only are eggs normally sold at a higher price in the east than in the prairies, but far more eggs are sold in the east than in the west. Therefore, in determining the national weighted average market price, the price-raising effect of the larger eastern marketings is considerably greater than the price-reducing effect of the smaller western marketings. The net result is that the national average price is raised a little, simply because more eggs are marketed in the east. And, to the extent that this price is raised, the amount of the deficiency payment is reduced.
In connection with table 2, it will be noted that the relationship between the support and market prices in the year 1962-63 was such that no deficiency payment was called for- and this whether the regional or national basis of administration had been used. Of course, this is because the average market price for the year is higher than the support price in every province, as well as in Canada as a whole. In addition to all the other reasons for not making the payments on a regional basis, there is the very practical difficulty of deciding how many regions there should be, and where a region should begin and end. If the regional basis were adopted, rational procedure would probably result in dividing the country into at least four or five regions. Apart from the fact that any such division would add greatly to the administra-

The motion before us suggests that the stabilization act be amended so as to provide for regional price support and semi-annual deficiency payments. The hon. member who put it forward stated that there had been a misunderstanding of some sort in connection with this whole idea. But the argument I wish to advance is directed to the impracticability of making semi-annual payments.
The legislation, of course, does not have to be changed to provide for these features. They can be introduced under the act as it now stands. To amend the act to provide for regional supports or for semi-annual deficiency payments would be meaningful only if it was intended to have the law require that price supports be on a regional basis and that deficiency payments be made semiannually. If that is the intent of the motion, it could present some very serious difficulties.
While the motion mentions eggs and hogs it also adds the word "et cetera", and presumably the intention would be to apply it to all products which are on a deficiency payment basis of support.

subtopic: DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS ON CUMULATED REGIONAL PRICE BASIS
speechtext: I point out that the stabilization board already has authority to authorize payments on a regional basis or on a semi-annual basis. I do not think the act would have to be changed.

subtopic: DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS ON CUMULATED REGIONAL PRICE BASIS
speechtext:
That is what I said. But it would be quite impractical to do this. It would be altogether impractical to make semi-annual deficiency payments for such seasonal crops as sugar beets, or soybeans, or Ontario wheat, or tobacco, to mention a few products which are under deficiency payments and are produced only once each year. After the marketing year for such crops is over, the average returns to producers are calculated and if these are below the support level a deficiency payment is made. There would be no practical way in which these payments could be made semi-annually.
There are some other questionable features of the motion, even if it were intended to apply specifically to eggs and hogs. It suggests that deficiency payments be "on a cumulated regional price basis rather than on a national weighted average price".
There are two components of a deficiency payment. One is the support level. The other is the average price which producers receive. If the average price received by producers is less than the support price, a deficiency payment is made for the amount of the difference. At present, for example, the support
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Batten).]
level is 34 cents per dozen for grade A large eggs and 23.65 cents per pound for grade A hogs. These are national average support prices. If the weighted national average price received by producers during the year is below those support prices there is a deficiency payment.
The motion, though, appears to deal with only one of the components of the deficiency payment calculation. It seems to deal only with the price received by producers, and suggests that this should be calculated on a cumulated regional price basis. This appears to assume that if Saskatchewan, for example, were established as a region for eggs, the amount of the deficiency payment would be the difference between the 34 cent support price and the cumulated price received by producers in Saskatchewan. This would not be so. The 34 cent support price is a national average price. It is an averaging of prices in the higher priced regions, such as Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia, with those in lower priced regions, such as Saskatchewan. If we were to have regional price supports, then both the support price and the price paid to producers would have to be based on prices in that region. The support price for Saskatchewan under that arrangement would be much lower than the present 34 cent national support price.

speechtext: How could our price be lower than it is today? The hon. member said it would be lower on a regional basis. The price is 17 cents a dozen for grade A large eggs now. How could it be any lower?

subtopic: DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS ON CUMULATED REGIONAL PRICE BASIS

If you work it out on a regional average price as compared with the national price, it will be lower. In general, changing both the support level and the calculation of producers' returns to a regional basis would not change the situation in different areas very much from what it is now on a national basis. Then, of course, there is the problem of deciding how to define a region. This is one of the real difficulties in working out a regional basis of support. It would hardly be practicable to rely on provincial boundaries. A great many Saskatchewan hogs, for example, are marketed in Manitoba. If the principle was extended to cattle, where would a region begin and end anywhere in the west or, for that matter, anywhere other than nationally? It has to end nationally.
The same difficulty exists with the proposal for semi-annual deficiency payments, even for commodities like eggs and hogs which are marketed throughout the year. Here it seems

to be generally assumed that deficiency payments would be based on the annual support price. But this could not be so. Just as there are areas where eggs and hogs prices are normally lower than in other areas, so with both eggs and hogs there are seasons when prices are higher or lower than in other seasons. If there were to be semi-annual deficiency payments, the support price would have to be calculated on a 10-year average price for those six months, and not for the full year.
